questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following is not a boundary of the hepatocystic triangle?
questions.concept: The hepatocystic (Calot's) triangle is bounded by the cystic duct, the common hepatic duct and the inferior surface of the liver. The cystic artery runs within this triangle as its key content, so it is not a boundary.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which nerve defect causes lagophthalmos?
questions.concept: Lagophthalmos (inability to fully close the eye) results from facial nerve (CN VII) palsy, which paralyses orbicularis oculi, the muscle that closes the eyelids.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which nerve innervates the lateral rectus muscle?
questions.concept: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (CN VI) - remember 'LR6 SO4': lateral rectus = 6th, superior oblique = 4th, and all other extraocular muscles = oculomotor (3rd).

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient presented to OPD with ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. Diagnosis of superior orbital fissure syndrome was confirmed after examination. Which nerves are compressed in this case?
questions.concept: The superior orbital fissure transmits cranial nerves III, IV, V1 (ophthalmic) and VI plus the ophthalmic veins; a lesion here gives ophthalmoplegia and ptosis. The optic nerve (II) passes the optic canal and the maxillary nerve (V2) the foramen rotundum, so neither traverses the fissure.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient has a 'down and out' right eye with ptosis, present since birth. Which nerve palsy is this?
questions.concept: An eye that is depressed and abducted ('down and out') with ptosis reflects loss of the oculomotor (CN III) supply to the medial/superior/inferior recti, inferior oblique and levator palpebrae superioris, leaving the intact lateral rectus (CN VI) and superior oblique (CN IV) unopposed. CN IV and CN VI palsies do not cause ptosis or this position, and CN VII affects facial muscles.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient shows unilateral facial droop with inability to close the eye and loss of forehead wrinkling on the affected side. Which of the following is most likely involved?
questions.concept: Unilateral facial droop with inability to close the eye and loss of forehead wrinkling is a lower-motor-neuron facial (7th cranial nerve) palsy, i.e. Bell's palsy. A 3rd-nerve palsy causes ptosis/ophthalmoplegia, and Erb's palsy is a brachial-plexus (arm) injury.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which of the following nerves gives sensory supply to the orbit?
questions.concept: Sensory innervation of the orbit is provided by the trigeminal nerve through its ophthalmic (V1) and maxillary (V2) divisions; the oculomotor nerve is motor, and the vagus and hypoglossal nerves do not supply the orbit.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: The stapedial (acoustic) reflex depends on the integrity of which cranial nerve for its motor response?
questions.concept: The stapedial reflex protects the inner ear from loud sound. Its afferent limb is the cochlear nerve (CN VIII); its efferent (motor) limb is the facial nerve (CN VII) via the nerve to stapedius. A proximal facial nerve lesion abolishes the reflex and can cause hyperacusis. The tensor tympani reflex uses CN V.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which muscle movements are related to the Abducens nerve?
questions.concept: The abducens nerve (CN VI) supplies only the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye; its palsy causes a convergent (medial) squint with failure of abduction.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: What is the primary action of the muscle originating from this structure?
questions.concept: The only option describing depression (opening) of the mandible fits the lateral pterygoid, which protracts and depresses the mandible; elevation/retraction actions belong to masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid. NOTE: this is an image-based item and the originating structure could not be seen, so the answer is inferred from the option pattern and left unverified.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A patient with a pituitary adenoma compressing the optic chiasm presents with loss of visual field. What visual field defect will be seen?
questions.concept: A pituitary adenoma compresses the central optic chiasm, damaging the decussating nasal-retinal fibres from both eyes, which carry the temporal visual fields, producing bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract lesions instead cause homonymous hemianopia.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: After the parotidectomy operation, a patient presents with excessive sweating and redness over the parotid region. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Frey's syndrome (gustatory sweating and facial flushing over the parotid region on eating) follows parotidectomy when the injured auriculotemporal nerve regenerates aberrantly, wiring parasympathetic salivary fibres to the skin's sweat glands. Horner's syndrome instead causes loss (not excess) of sweating.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A young man presents with weakness of the entire right side of his face - drooping of the right angle of the mouth with inability to raise the right eyebrow or close the right eye. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
options: Supranuclear facial palsy on the right side
Supranuclear facial palsy on the left side
Infranuclear facial palsy on the left side
Infranuclear facial palsy on the right side
questions.concept: Involvement of the forehead (inability to raise the eyebrow and close the eye) along with the lower face on the same side indicates a lower-motor-neuron (infranuclear) facial nerve palsy on the right. An upper-motor-neuron lesion spares the forehead due to bilateral cortical input. NOTE: the recalled stem was garbled ('both sides'); the intended picture is unilateral right whole-face weakness.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A child presents with telecanthus, hypertelorism, antimongoloid slant, and cardiac defects. What is the most likely chromosomal abnormality?
questions.concept: This picture (facial dysmorphism with hypertelorism plus conotruncal cardiac defects, and often hypocalcaemia/thymic aplasia) is DiGeorge / velocardiofacial syndrome, caused by a microdeletion at chromosome 22q11.2 - a defect of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: Which nerve is most commonly injured in fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus?
questions.concept: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, so fractures/dislocations there commonly injure it, causing deltoid paralysis (impaired abduction) and sensory loss over the 'regimental badge' area of the upper lateral arm.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman has tingling of the lateral three digits with loss of sensation over the base of the thumb on the dorsal aspect of the hand. Which nerve is involved?
questions.concept: Sensory loss over the dorsal aspect of the base of the thumb and the first web space localises to the superficial branch of the radial nerve, which supplies the dorsum of the lateral hand. The median nerve supplies the palmar surface (and dorsal fingertips) of the lateral three-and-a-half digits, not the dorsal thumb base.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.topic: Lower limb: femoral/sciatic nerve, foot drop
questions.stem: A man sustained trauma on the lateral side of his right knee. Two days later, he complains of difficulty in walking, as his toes keep dragging on the ground. He also notices numbness over the upper lateral aspect of the leg and dorsum of the foot. Which nerve is most likely injured?
questions.concept: The common peroneal (fibular) nerve is superficial at the neck of the fibula on the lateral knee, so trauma there causes foot drop (loss of dorsiflexion/eversion) with sensory loss over the upper lateral leg and dorsum of the foot. The deep peroneal branch alone would not explain the wider lateral-leg sensory loss.

questions.subject: Anatomy
questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a history of cyanosis since infancy. Which of the following is a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.concept: Tetralogy of Fallot comprises a VSD, an overriding aorta, right ventricular outflow (infundibular pulmonary) stenosis and right ventricular hypertrophy. Of the options, infundibular pulmonary stenosis is the true component; the defect is a VSD (not ASD) and the hypertrophy is right- (not left-) ventricular.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following amino acids primarily acts as a buffer in blood due to its ability to accept and donate protons at physiological pH?
questions.concept: Histidine's imidazole side chain has a pKa near 6.0, close to physiological pH, so it readily accepts and donates protons, making histidine (and the histidine residues of haemoglobin) the main amino-acid buffer of blood. Arginine (pKa about 12.5) and tyrosine (pKa about 10) are poor buffers at pH 7.4.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Cancer cells take up excess glucose because?
options: Lactate is produced even in the presence of oxygen
questions.concept: This is the Warburg effect: tumour cells preferentially perform aerobic glycolysis, producing lactate even when oxygen is available, which drives high glucose uptake to meet biosynthetic and energy demands.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient presents with arthritis, and arthroscopy reveals blackening of the joints. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible for this condition?
questions.concept: Arthritis with blackening of joints (ochronosis) is alkaptonuria, due to deficiency of homogentisate oxidase; homogentisic acid accumulates and deposits in cartilage and joints, and the urine darkens on standing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following is deficient in the mucopolysaccharidosis associated with Natowicz disease?
questions.concept: Natowicz disease is mucopolysaccharidosis type IX, caused by hyaluronidase deficiency, so hyaluronic acid (a non-sulfated GAG) accumulates. NOTE: the stem says 'deficient' but the intended answer is the GAG involved/accumulated (hyaluronic acid); the deficient enzyme is hyaluronidase.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child presents with fatigue and hepatomegaly. Liver enzymes (ALT, AST) are elevated and ketosis is significant. Liver biopsy shows excess glycogen accumulation. Blood glucose rises after feeding but there is no rise after an overnight fast. Which enzyme deficiency is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: Fasting hypoglycaemia with no glucose rise on fasting, hepatomegaly and hepatic glycogen overload indicates glucose-6-phosphatase deficiency (von Gierke, GSD type I): the final common step that releases free glucose from both glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis is blocked, whereas absorbed dietary glucose can still raise blood sugar.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A man presents with high VLDL and chylomicrons, with eruptive xanthomas. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Markedly raised VLDL and chylomicrons with eruptive xanthomas indicate severe hypertriglyceridaemia (familial hypertriglyceridaemia), which carries a pancreatitis risk. Familial hypercholesterolaemia instead raises LDL with tendon xanthomas, and dysbetalipoproteinaemia raises IDL/remnants.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding Bempedoic acid are correct?
options: It is used along with diet and statins for hypercholesterolemia
It is a non-competitive inhibitor of ATP citrate lyase
questions.concept: Bempedoic acid is a dicarboxylic-acid prodrug that inhibits ATP citrate lyase, reducing cholesterol synthesis upstream of HMG-CoA reductase, and is used with diet and statins for hypercholesterolaemia. NOTE: as worded (which are correct), options B, C and D are all essentially true and even A is partly right (it does inhibit ATP citrate lyase, though 'non-competitive' is dubious); the scraped single answer B is correct but not unique - so flagged.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A girl presents with microcephaly and a high-pitched cry. Which of the following is the most likely chromosomal abnormality?
questions.concept: Microcephaly with a shrill, high-pitched 'cat-like' cry is cri-du-chat syndrome, caused by a deletion of the short arm of chromosome 5 (5p-).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A child with fused carpal bones comes to your clinic. What is the gene associated with hand-foot (hand-foot-genital) syndrome?
questions.concept: Hand-Foot-Genital syndrome (distal limb malformations - here fused/short carpals and short thumbs/great toes - with genitourinary anomalies) is caused by a mutation in the HOXA13 homeobox gene. BCL6 links to lymphoma, FGFR to skeletal dysplasias, and COL11 to hearing loss/Stickler syndrome.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A 7-year-old child of short stature presents with skin patches and learning difficulties. Diagnostic workup indicates a defect in DNA repair specifically related to double-strand breaks. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Bloom syndrome is caused by a defective BLM RecQ helicase needed for homologous-recombination repair of double-strand breaks, producing chromosomal instability, marked short stature, photosensitive facial erythema/cafe-au-lait patches and cancer predisposition. XP and Cockayne are nucleotide-excision-repair defects and Lynch is a mismatch-repair defect, so the 'double-strand break' clue uniquely selects Bloom.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency can lead to lactic acidosis?
questions.concept: Thiamine (vitamin B1) is the cofactor of pyruvate dehydrogenase; in deficiency pyruvate cannot enter the TCA cycle and is diverted to lactate, producing lactic acidosis (seen with beriberi and Wernicke's encephalopathy).

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency is associated with scurvy?
questions.concept: Scurvy is caused by vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency; ascorbate is a cofactor for prolyl/lysyl hydroxylase in collagen synthesis, so deficiency yields defective collagen with bleeding gums, perifollicular haemorrhages and poor wound healing.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency causes defective clotting and bleeding tendencies?
questions.concept: Vitamin K is the cofactor for gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S); its deficiency prevents their activation and causes a bleeding tendency with a prolonged PT.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient with chronic alcoholism presents with confusion, ataxia, and ophthalmoplegia. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?
questions.concept: The triad of confusion, ataxia and ophthalmoplegia in an alcoholic is Wernicke encephalopathy from thiamine (B1) deficiency; thiamine is a cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and transketolase, and glucose must not be given before thiamine or the deficiency is precipitated/worsened.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient whose diet mainly consists of pulses and rice presents with bowed legs (stick deformity). Which vitamin could have prevented this condition?
questions.concept: Bowed legs from defective bone mineralisation is rickets, caused by vitamin D deficiency (a rice-and-pulses diet is low in vitamin D and calcium). Vitamin D drives intestinal calcium/phosphate absorption and bone mineralisation. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness, C scurvy, and B12 megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: A patient presents with gum bleeding, petechiae, poor wound healing, and other related symptoms. Which of the following vitamin deficiencies is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.concept: Bleeding gums, petechiae and poor wound healing are classic for scurvy (vitamin C deficiency); vitamin C is needed for collagen synthesis, so its lack gives fragile capillaries and defective connective-tissue repair.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes is dependent on Vitamin C for its activity?
questions.concept: Prolyl (and lysyl) hydroxylase need vitamin C as a cofactor to hydroxylate proline/lysine residues, stabilising collagen; lysyl oxidase, in contrast, is copper-dependent, not vitamin C-dependent.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which of the following deficiencies causes follicular hyperkeratosis?
questions.concept: Follicular hyperkeratosis (phrynoderma, 'toad skin') is the classic cutaneous sign of vitamin A deficiency, reflecting keratinising metaplasia of the follicular epithelium.

questions.subject: Biochemistry
questions.stem: Which vitamin deficiency leads to night blindness?
questions.concept: Vitamin A (as retinal) is the chromophore of rhodopsin in rod photoreceptors; its deficiency impairs rod function first, causing night blindness (nyctalopia) as the earliest sign, later progressing to conjunctival xerosis, Bitot spots and keratomalacia.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A person was found dead in a swimming pool. On autopsy, the stomach and lungs were filled with water, and there was mucoid froth at the nose and mouth. What is the most likely mode of death?
questions.concept: Water in the lungs and stomach with copious, persistent fine froth at the mouth and nose indicates wet drowning, where aspirated water washes out surfactant causing alveolar collapse and hypoxaemia. Dry drowning is death from laryngospasm with essentially dry lungs.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: After a road traffic accident, NCCT head was normal on admission. The patient later died in the ICU following coma, and brain biopsy revealed multiple punctate haemorrhages. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A high-speed head injury with a normal initial CT but prolonged coma and multiple deep punctate white-matter haemorrhages is diffuse axonal injury, caused by shearing/rotational forces tearing axons in the white matter, corpus callosum and brainstem. Subdural bleeds are crescentic on CT and ischaemic infarcts give territorial hypodensity, not scattered petechiae.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A villager assaulted by 4-5 people is brought to hospital in serious condition and his dying declaration is being taken. Which of the following is correct regarding this process?
options: A doctor can record the statement
A Magistrate can record the statement
Oath is compulsory before recording the statement
questions.concept: A dying declaration is ideally recorded by a Magistrate; no oath is administered and leading questions must be avoided. NOTE: option B (a doctor may record it, e.g. when a Magistrate is unavailable) is also true, so the item is ambiguous - the exam key is A.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A person who was mentally unsound at the time of committing a crime is exempt from liability if they were unaware of the nature of their actions or its consequences. What is this principle called?
questions.concept: The McNaughton (M'Naghten) rule is the legal test of insanity: a person is not criminally liable if, due to unsoundness of mind, they did not know the nature of the act or that it was wrong.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: What is the minimum age at which a woman can give valid consent for Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) in India?
questions.concept: Under the MTP Act a woman aged 18 years or older can give valid consent for termination herself; for a minor (below 18) or a mentally ill woman, the written consent of a guardian is required.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A forensic expert receives a district-court summons to give evidence in a criminal case, but two days earlier had already received a summons for a civil case in the same district court on the same date. What should the doctor do?
options: Attend the court for which the summons came first
Attend the court for the criminal case
questions.concept: When summoned to both a criminal and a civil court for the same date, the doctor must attend the criminal court first, as criminal proceedings take precedence over civil; the civil court is informed and attended later.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A married female dies in unnatural circumstances within 3 years of marriage. Her father files a report to police and inquiry will be done under which section?
questions.concept: Unnatural death of a married woman within 7 years of marriage triggers a Magistrate's inquiry into the cause of death under Section 176 CrPC, now Section 196 BNSS (option B). Section 174 CrPC / 194 BNSS is the ordinary police inquest.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A married female dies within 3 years of marriage. The inquest is done by?
questions.concept: Unnatural or suspicious death of a married woman within 7 years of marriage mandates a Magistrate's inquest (not police or coroner) because of the risk of a dowry-related death. The coroner system no longer operates in India.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: Leading questions can be asked in?
questions.concept: Leading questions are permitted during cross-examination; they are not allowed in examination-in-chief or re-examination except with the court's permission.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: As per the MTP (Amendment) Act, 2021, the opinion of two registered medical practitioners is required for termination of pregnancy at which gestational age?
questions.concept: Under the MTP (Amendment) Act 2021, termination up to 20 weeks needs the opinion of one registered medical practitioner, while 20-24 weeks (for specified categories of women) requires the opinion of two RMPs.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.topic: Legal procedure, consent, key IPC sections
questions.stem: A doctor receives two summons, one to appear in court in a murder case and another to provide expert medical opinion. Which of the following should the doctor prioritise?
options: Appearance for providing medical expert opinion
questions.concept: When a doctor holds two summonses at once, the one from the higher/criminal court takes precedence; a Sessions Court summons in a murder trial therefore outranks a request merely to furnish an expert opinion. Timing of receipt does not override the legal gravity of the criminal-case summons.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A body brought for autopsy is cold and has developed rigor mortis in all 4 limbs and livor mortis at the back/fixed, but no signs of putrefaction. What will be the estimated time since death?
questions.concept: Combining the postmortem signs, a cold body with rigor fully established in all four limbs (about 12 h, persisting to 24-36 h), fixed livor (fixed by 6-12 h) and no putrefaction (begins about 24-36 h) places the time since death at roughly 12-24 hours.

questions.subject: Forensic Medicine (FMT)
questions.stem: A deceased woman was sent for an autopsy. She was found dead in a locked room with a heat stove still running. What is the most likely cause of death?
questions.concept: A body found in a closed room with a running fuel stove points to carbon monoxide poisoning from incomplete combustion; CO binds haemoglobin ~200-250x more avidly than oxygen, causing tissue hypoxia despite a normal PaO2 and the classic cherry-red post-mortem lividity.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A farmer presents with fever and subconjunctival hemorrhage. The microscopic agglutination test turns out to be positive. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: A farmer/water-exposed patient with fever and conjunctival suffusion or subconjunctival haemorrhage in whom the microscopic agglutination test (MAT, the gold standard) is positive has leptospirosis (Leptospira interrogans, a gram-negative spirochete). Brucella instead uses the standard serum tube agglutination test, not MAT.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient's labs are positive for malarial antigen, and the Widal test shows O antigen >1:300, H antigen >1:20, A >1:20, B >1:20. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A markedly raised Widal O-agglutinin titre (>1:300) with low H and paratyphoid titres indicates a recent Salmonella (enteric fever) infection; a rise in only H suggests convalescence/anamnestic response, and a rise in all H antigens suggests prior TAB vaccination.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which organism is the most common cause of urinary tract infection in females?
questions.concept: Escherichia coli (a uropathogenic gram-negative bacillus) is by far the commonest cause of uncomplicated urinary tract infection in women, aided by fimbrial (P-fimbriae) adhesins that let it colonise the urothelium.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A woman presents with sudden-onset high-grade fever, hypotension, a diffuse rash, and a history of using a tampon for an extended period. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Sudden high fever, hypotension and a diffuse erythrodermic rash (with later desquamation) after prolonged tampon use is toxic shock syndrome, mediated by the Staphylococcus aureus superantigen TSST-1 (occasionally group A streptococcus), which triggers massive T-cell activation and cytokine release.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 30-year-old man develops profuse vomiting and diarrhea within 3 hours of consuming pre-packaged salad and milk at a picnic. There is no fever. Which of the following is the most likely causative organism?
questions.concept: Sudden vomiting and diarrhoea within 1-6 hours of eating dairy/salad foods, without fever, is caused by the preformed heat-stable enterotoxins of Staphylococcus aureus; because it is toxin-mediated, onset is rapid and the illness is self-limited. Clostridium perfringens and Salmonella have longer incubation periods.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: MOA of botulinum toxin is:
questions.concept: Botulinum toxin (from Clostridium botulinum) acts by inhibiting acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing flaccid paralysis. Contrast: diphtheria and Pseudomonas exotoxin A inhibit elongation factor-2; tetanus toxin blocks GABA/glycine release (spastic paralysis); cholera and pertussis toxins raise cAMP.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman underwent elective surgery 10 days ago and received broad-spectrum intravenous clindamycin. She now presents with profuse watery diarrhea. Which organism is the primary cause?
questions.concept: Clindamycin is a classic precipitant of Clostridioides difficile infection, a gram-positive spore-forming anaerobe whose toxins A and B cause antibiotic-associated pseudomembranous colitis with profuse watery diarrhoea.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which organism is most commonly responsible for gas gangrene?
questions.concept: Gas gangrene (clostridial myonecrosis) is most often caused by Clostridium perfringens (type A), whose alpha-toxin (a lecithinase) destroys cell membranes and produces crepitant, gas-filled necrotic muscle. C. difficile causes pseudomembranous colitis, C. tetani spastic paralysis, and C. botulinum flaccid paralysis.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the culture media used for tuberculosis?
questions.concept: Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the standard egg-based solid medium for culturing Mycobacterium tuberculosis; MacConkey, blood and chocolate agar are used for other bacteria.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient with HIV presents with bouts of cough and fever. Which medium is most appropriate for diagnosis?
questions.concept: In an HIV patient with cough and fever, TB is the prime suspect; Lowenstein-Jensen (LJ) medium is the classic solid culture medium for Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Tinsdale and Loeffler serum slope grow Corynebacterium diphtheriae, and MacConkey grows gram-negative enterics.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The toughness of bacterial cell walls is due to:
questions.concept: The rigidity/toughness of the bacterial cell wall comes from peptidoglycan (murein), the cross-linked NAM-NAG mesh that resists osmotic lysis. Teichoic acid, LPS and the outer membrane serve other roles and are not the source of mechanical strength.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A woman was bitten by a rabid dog. The dog developed symptoms and died within a week. What is the best method for antemortem diagnosis of rabies?
questions.concept: The direct fluorescent antibody test (DFAT) is the standard antemortem test for rabies, detecting viral antigen in corneal smears, nuchal skin biopsy (hair follicles), or saliva. Negri bodies and Seller's stain are histologic (postmortem) findings; brain biopsy is invasive and not used antemortem.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: What is the usual method of collecting a sample of urine to detect UTI?
questions.concept: A clean-catch midstream sample is the usual, least-invasive way to collect urine for suspected UTI because it minimises contamination by peri-urethral commensals; early-morning samples are for proteinuria and initial-stream samples are contamination-prone.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which antibody is the first to appear and acts fastest during a primary (first) immune response to an infection?
questions.concept: IgM is the first antibody produced in the primary immune response; as a pentamer with 10 binding sites it has high avidity and activates the classical complement pathway efficiently, even before affinity maturation. IgG dominates the secondary response.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent bacterial and fungal infections, chronic diarrhea, and failure to thrive. He is diagnosed with severe combined immunodeficiency due to an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. Which enzyme deficiency is responsible?
questions.concept: The commonest autosomal-recessive severe combined immunodeficiency is adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; accumulated deoxyadenosine/dATP is toxic to both T and B lymphocytes, causing recurrent bacterial, viral and fungal infections. (HGPRT deficiency causes Lesch-Nyhan; OTC deficiency causes hyperammonaemia.)

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which cell type is primarily responsible for antibody production?
questions.concept: Plasma cells are terminally differentiated B lymphocytes and are the factories of antibody (immunoglobulin) secretion; T cells help/regulate the response but do not themselves secrete antibody.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A child presents with recurrent Staphylococcus infections. Laboratory examination shows very low levels of immunoglobulins (G, A, M, E) and a low quantity of B cells. There is a normal reaction to environmental antigens on the skin. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Very low levels of all immunoglobulin classes with absent/low B cells but preserved T-cell function (a normal delayed-hypersensitivity skin reaction) is Bruton X-linked agammaglobulinaemia. Hyper-IgM has normal/high IgM, and CVID usually presents later with normal B-cell numbers.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A 27-year-old pregnant female in her first trimester presents to the OPD for a regular antenatal checkup. During blood type screening, potential ABO incompatibility is discussed. The healthcare provider explains that certain antibody types are less concerning than others during pregnancy. ABO incompatibility does not occur due to which antibody in her case?
questions.concept: ABO haemolytic disease of the newborn is caused by maternal IgG anti-A/anti-B crossing the placenta; naturally occurring ABO isohaemagglutinins are IgM, and IgD is not a blood-group antibody at all, so incompatibility never arises from IgD. NOTE: the wording is ambiguous - the inferred key is IgD (the isotype never involved in ABO antibodies), but a reader focused on placental transfer could defensibly pick IgM (does not cross the placenta), so this item is flagged for manual review.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which opportunistic pathogen demonstrates a "crushed ping pong ball appearance" on Gomori methenamine stain?
questions.concept: Pneumocystis jirovecii cysts show a 'crushed ping-pong ball' (also cup-and-saucer/helmet) appearance on Gomori methenamine silver stain and cause pneumonia in the immunocompromised (e.g. HIV with CD4 <200); treatment is co-trimoxazole.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A baby is born with microcephaly, intracerebral calcification and chorioretinitis. Which teratogenic infection is the mother suffering from?
questions.concept: The combination of chorioretinitis, diffuse intracranial calcification and hydrocephalus/microcephaly in a neonate suggests congenital toxoplasmosis (Toxoplasma gondii, a protozoan). NOTE: CMV overlaps but classically gives periventricular calcification with sensorineural deafness.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A patient is positive for HBsAg and anti-HBc IgM. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: HBsAg positivity together with anti-HBc of the IgM class indicates acute hepatitis B (highly infectious). IgG anti-HBc with HBsAg denotes chronic infection; isolated anti-HBs indicates vaccination; and isolated IgM anti-HBc marks the window period.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the characteristic lesion of Kaposi sarcoma?
options: A white, striated lesion that cannot be scraped off
questions.concept: Kaposi sarcoma (caused by HHV-8, an AIDS-defining malignancy) presents as violaceous, raised purple-red macules, plaques and nodules, the colour reflecting proliferating vessels with extravasated red cells and haemosiderin. A pus-filled yellow lesion is bacterial, and a white non-scrapable striated plaque describes leukoplakia/lichen planus.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: The receptor used for the entry of HIV into the host cell is?
questions.concept: HIV enters host CD4+ cells by binding gp120 to CD4 plus a chemokine co-receptor; among the options CCR5 (used by macrophage-tropic strains) is correct, and the CCR5-delta32 mutation confers resistance. CD4, the main receptor, is not among the options.

questions.subject: Microbiology
questions.stem: A TB patient with HIV begins ART and experiences deterioration in health after 2 months. What is the likely cause?
options: Development of drug resistance to TB drugs
Development of drug resistance to ART
Drug-drug interactions between TB and ART medications
questions.concept: Deterioration a few weeks to months after starting ART in an HIV-TB patient is immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS): recovering CD4 function mounts an exaggerated inflammatory response against the existing TB. Both TB treatment and ART are continued, with NSAIDs/steroids if severe.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: A diabetic male presents with seizures. Imaging shows a brain lesion and histopathology reveals liquefactive necrosis. What is the most important mechanism responsible?
questions.concept: Liquefactive necrosis (typical of brain and abscesses) is driven by hydrolytic/lysosomal enzyme digestion released by microglia and neutrophils; the lipid-rich, stroma-poor brain rapidly liquefies. Even when the trigger is ischaemia or infection, the necrosis type in the CNS is liquefactive and the mechanism is enzymatic breakdown.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: Which of the following is a change seen in irreversible cell injury?
questions.concept: Large amorphous (flocculent) densities within mitochondria are a morphological hallmark of irreversible cell injury, reflecting severe mitochondrial membrane damage; membrane blebbing, chromatin clumping and cellular (hydropic) swelling are features of reversible injury.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: Which of the following acts as a major intracellular antioxidant and helps in detoxifying reactive oxygen species?
questions.concept: Glutathione is the major intracellular antioxidant (a glutamate-cysteine-glycine tripeptide) that neutralises reactive oxygen species by donating electrons and helps regenerate vitamins C and E. SOD, catalase and peroxidases are the antioxidant enzymes that act on specific radicals.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Cell injury, adaptation, necrosis vs apoptosis
questions.stem: In Barrett's oesophagus, which of the following epithelial transformations occurs?
questions.concept: Barrett's oesophagus is a complication of chronic GERD in which the distal oesophageal stratified squamous epithelium undergoes intestinal-type metaplasia (columnar epithelium with goblet cells). This adaptive metaplasia raises the risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A skin graft was performed on an immunocompromised patient using tissue from another immunocompromised individual. Weeks later the patient developed contractures and systemic symptoms. What is the most likely cause?
options: Rejection due to recipient T8 cells
questions.concept: When immunocompetent donor lymphocytes are transferred into a recipient who cannot reject them (immunocompromised host), the donor T cells attack host tissues: graft-versus-host disease, giving systemic features (fever, rash, hepatitis, diarrhoea) plus sclerodermatous skin contractures. Host-versus-graft rejection requires an immunocompetent recipient, and graft failure/necrosis occurs early without systemic immune features.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: All of the following are correct about NETs except?
questions.concept: Neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) are webs of decondensed chromatin studded with antimicrobial proteins, formed by NETosis (which requires PAD4-mediated citrullination of arginine residues on histones) and implicated in sepsis and in exposing autoantigens that drive SLE. They trap microbes extracellularly and are NOT a form of phagocytosis - hence the 'except'.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: In a follow-up case of prostate cancer, what do we need to check?
questions.concept: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is the marker of choice for monitoring treated prostate cancer - a rising PSA signals biochemical recurrence or progression. Alkaline phosphatase (bone metastases) and prostatic acid phosphatase (outdated) are not used for routine follow-up.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A patient with chronic smoking presents with hemoptysis and weight loss. Which lung cancer is most commonly associated with smoking?
questions.concept: Among the options, squamous cell carcinoma has the strongest association with smoking; it is typically central (arising in main bronchi), presents with haemoptysis, and may cause hypercalcaemia via PTHrP. (Small cell carcinoma is even more tightly smoking-linked but was not offered.)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with progressive difficulty climbing stairs and rising from a chair develops fatigue and falls after walking for some time. Chest imaging reveals a hilar lung mass. Which of the following is the most likely type of lung cancer associated with this patient's condition?
questions.concept: Proximal muscle weakness in the setting of a central/hilar lung mass points to Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome, a paraneoplastic disorder caused by autoantibodies against presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels, most strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which of the following enzymes is typically elevated in prostate cancer?
questions.concept: Prostatic acid phosphatase rises in prostate cancer, especially with bone metastases (an older tumour marker now largely replaced by PSA). ALP rises in bone/liver disease, LDH is non-specific, and AFP marks hepatocellular and germ-cell tumours.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A patient with a 3-month history of cough and weight loss has a lung mass whose biopsy expresses chromogranin and synaptophysin. Which paraneoplastic syndrome is most likely?
questions.concept: Chromogranin and synaptophysin positivity identifies a neuroendocrine tumour, here small cell lung carcinoma, which classically secretes ectopic ADH producing SIADH and dilutional hyponatraemia. Ectopic ACTH/Cushing also occurs with small cell carcinoma but SIADH is the single best answer, while PTHrP-mediated hypercalcaemia belongs to squamous cell carcinoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 14-year-old boy presents with pain and swelling over the lower leg for 2 months. X-ray shows an onion-skin periosteal reaction. Biopsy reveals PAS-positive small round blue cells. Which of the following chromosomal translocations is most commonly associated with this tumor?
questions.concept: Onion-skin periosteal reaction with PAS-positive small round blue cells in an adolescent is Ewing sarcoma, driven by t(11;22)(q24;q12), which fuses EWSR1 (chromosome 22) with FLI1 (chromosome 11) to form the EWSR1-FLI1 fusion oncoprotein. For contrast: t(9;22) = CML, t(8;14) = Burkitt lymphoma, t(15;17) = acute promyelocytic leukaemia.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT related to progression of a (basal cell) cancer?
questions.concept: In grading a cancer's aggressiveness, depth of invasion, anatomical site and stage all determine progression and prognosis, whereas the mere duration of the lesion does not directly indicate progression (as with slow-growing basal cell carcinoma). NOTE: the source stem omits the basal-cell-carcinoma context that appears only in the explanation.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which occupational exposure is most strongly associated with mesothelioma?
questions.concept: Asbestos fibres (especially crocidolite) lodge in the pleura and, after a long latency (20-40 years), cause malignant mesothelioma - the tumour most specifically linked to asbestos. Silica causes silicosis, cotton dust byssinosis and coal dust coal-workers' pneumoconiosis, none of which is strongly linked to mesothelioma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man presents with progressive weight loss, altered bowel habits, and intermittent passage of blood in stools for 4 months. Colonoscopy reveals an ulceroproliferative growth in the sigmoid colon, and biopsy confirms adenocarcinoma of the colon. Mutation in which of the following genes is most commonly associated?
questions.concept: In the colonic adenoma-carcinoma sequence, KRAS is the classic oncogene activated after APC loss; among the options it is the mutation most commonly linked to colorectal adenocarcinoma. (APC is the single most frequently mutated gene overall but is not listed here.)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: Which correctly describes neoadjuvant chemotherapy?
questions.concept: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is given BEFORE the definitive/primary treatment (usually surgery) to downstage or shrink the tumour and improve resectability; chemotherapy given after surgery is termed adjuvant. (Scraped label was Anatomy; the tested concept is an oncology principle.)

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 60-year-old presents with an ulcer on the medial canthus having rolled-out, beaded margins. Histopathology shows nests of cells with a peripheral palisading pattern. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: An ulcer with rolled/beaded ('rodent ulcer') margins, classically at the medial canthus, showing islands/nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading on histology is basal cell carcinoma - the commonest skin cancer, locally invasive but rarely metastasising.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.topic: Neoplasia: grading vs staging, tumor markers
questions.stem: A 32-year-old man presents with a painless enlargement of the right testis for 3 months. There is no history of trauma or infection. Serum tumor markers show normal β-hCG and normal α-fetoprotein (AFP) levels. An image of the histopathology is provided below. Based on the clinical findings and histopathology, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Seminoma classically presents as a painless testicular mass with a NORMAL AFP (AFP is never raised in a pure seminoma) and histology of sheets of large cells with clear, glycogen-rich cytoplasm separated by fibrous septa infiltrated by lymphocytes. β-hCG may be mildly raised in a minority but AFP elevation would point instead to a yolk-sac/mixed tumour.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient presents with fatigue, anemia, and hepatomegaly. Hemoglobin electrophoresis reveals the presence of HbS. What will be the appropriate treatment?
questions.concept: HbS on electrophoresis indicates sickle cell anaemia; hydroxyurea is the mainstay disease-modifying therapy because it raises fetal haemoglobin (HbF), reducing sickling and vaso-occlusive crises. Transfusion is reserved for severe crises, and iron/B12 are not specific treatments.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old strict vegetarian presents with progressive fatigue, numbness and tingling in both feet, and difficulty walking for the past 6 months. Laboratory investigations reveal anemia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: A strict (vegan) vegetarian with anaemia plus a peripheral neuropathy / subacute combined degeneration picture indicates vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency, which produces a megaloblastic anaemia; the neurological features distinguish it from folate or iron deficiency.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 5-year-old child is brought to the clinic with abdominal pain, irritability, and developmental delay. On examination, the child has pallor and a bluish line on the gums. Laboratory tests reveal microcytic anemia, and a peripheral blood smear shows red blood cells with basophilic stippling. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Abdominal pain, developmental delay, a bluish gingival (Burton) line and microcytic anaemia with basophilic stippling indicate lead poisoning; manage by removing exposure and chelation (e.g. EDTA). Iron deficiency lacks stippling and the Burton line.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A patient has cheilosis with koilonychia and anaemia. What is the diagnosis?
questions.concept: Angular cheilosis and koilonychia with anaemia are signs of iron deficiency; the associated triad (with esophageal webs and glossitis) is Plummer-Vinson syndrome, which carries an increased risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. Achalasia and tylosis do not produce this iron-deficiency picture.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
questions.concept: Von Willebrand disease is the most common inherited bleeding disorder (usually autosomal, affecting both sexes); DIC is acquired, and haemophilia, though important, is less prevalent.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 46-year-old male presents to the outpatient department with a history of lower back pain and painful urination. Upon investigation, he is found to have normocytic normochromic anemia and hypercalcemia. Serum protein electrophoresis reveals an M-spike in the gamma region. Which of the following tests is most appropriate to confirm the diagnosis of multiple myeloma?
questions.concept: Multiple myeloma is confirmed by demonstrating monoclonal free light chains (Bence Jones protein) in urine alongside the serum M-spike, marrow plasmacytosis, hypercalcaemia, anaemia and lytic bone lesions; ordinary urine dipstick/UACR misses light chains.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the investigation of choice for CML?
questions.concept: CML is defined by the BCR-ABL fusion arising from t(9;22) (Philadelphia chromosome); FISH detects this fusion sensitively and is the investigation of choice among the given options. NOTE: conventional karyotyping is the traditional confirmatory test and RT-PCR (not listed) is the most sensitive method for diagnosis/monitoring; LAP score only distinguishes CML from a leukaemoid reaction.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A 2-year-old with fever, lymphadenopathy and biopsy showing hallmark cells is diagnosed with anaplastic large cell lymphoma. Most likely translocation?
questions.concept: Anaplastic large cell lymphoma characteristically carries the t(2;5) translocation creating the NPM-ALK fusion, which constitutively activates ALK tyrosine kinase; biopsy shows hallmark cells with horseshoe/kidney-shaped nuclei. t(8;14) is Burkitt, t(14;18) follicular lymphoma.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Tau protein inclusions are involved in:
questions.concept: Alzheimer's disease is characterised by intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau protein together with extracellular amyloid-beta plaques. Huntington's involves mutant huntingtin, and ALS involves SOD1/TDP-43, not tau.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: A child with Kawasaki disease develops multiple small coronary artery aneurysms. What is the treatment?
questions.concept: In Kawasaki disease with small coronary artery aneurysms, low-dose aspirin is continued for roughly 6-8 weeks (covering the high-thrombosis remodelling period) as small aneurysms often regress, alongside acute-phase IVIG. Lifelong aspirin is for giant/persistent aneurysms and about 4 weeks applies when there is no coronary involvement. NOTE: exact duration guidance varies (some continue antiplatelet until aneurysm regression), but among the options 6 weeks best fits small aneurysms.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the timing at which the triphenyl tetrazolium chloride can elicit findings post MI?
questions.concept: Triphenyltetrazolium chloride (TTC) stains viable myocardium (with intact dehydrogenases) brick-red and leaves infarcted tissue pale; it can demonstrate a myocardial infarct grossly by about 2-3 hours, earlier than routine light microscopy.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Which of the following is the earliest marker to rise in a case of myocardial infarction (MI)?
questions.concept: Heart-type fatty acid binding protein (H-FABP) is a small cytosolic protein released within 1-3 hours of myocardial injury, rising even earlier than CK-MB and troponin, making it the earliest of the listed markers; troponin remains the most specific/confirmatory.

questions.subject: Pathology
questions.stem: Increased unconjugated bilirubin with mild icterus is most commonly seen in:
questions.concept: Gilbert syndrome is a benign, common cause of mild unconjugated (indirect) hyperbilirubinaemia due to reduced UGT1A1 (glucuronyl transferase) activity, often unmasked by fasting/stress. Dubin-Johnson and Rotor cause CONJUGATED hyperbilirubinaemia; Crigler-Najjar causes severe unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia in the neonate.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is the treatment of choice for acute anaphylactic shock?
questions.concept: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first-line, life-saving drug in anaphylaxis: its alpha-1 action reverses vasodilatation and oedema while beta-1/beta-2 actions support the heart and relieve bronchospasm. Antihistamines and steroids are only adjuncts.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the preferred preoperative drug for managing blood pressure in a patient with pheochromocytoma?
questions.concept: Phenoxybenzamine, a long-acting irreversible non-selective alpha-blocker, is the classic preoperative agent for phaeochromocytoma to control BP and prevent intraoperative catecholamine surges; alpha blockade must precede any beta blockade to avoid unopposed alpha vasoconstriction.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A female patient with a history of bronchial asthma has developed an acute attack of migraine. Which drug should be avoided?
questions.concept: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-blocker (used for migraine prophylaxis) that must be avoided in asthmatics because beta-2 receptor blockade precipitates bronchospasm; the other listed agents are not contraindicated by asthma.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Scientists administered norepinephrine to guinea pigs, resulting in an increase in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and a decrease in heart rate. What mechanism explains this response?
questions.concept: Noradrenaline raises blood pressure by alpha-1 vasoconstriction; the rise stretches carotid/aortic baroreceptors, triggering a vagal reflex that slows the heart. This reflex bradycardia overrides noradrenaline's direct beta-1 cardiac stimulation.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which medication is used to reduce the frequency of future headache episodes in a 26-year-old woman with one-sided pulsating headaches accompanied by nausea, vomiting and photophobia, who finds relief in a dimly lit environment?
questions.concept: Unilateral pulsatile headache with nausea, photophobia and relief in a dark room is migraine; the beta-blocker propranolol is a drug of choice for migraine prophylaxis (reducing attack frequency). Triptans and ergots are for acute attacks, not prophylaxis.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 50-year-old male underwent lower abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia; vecuronium was administered as a muscle relaxant. At the end of surgery, which of the following is the most appropriate agent to reverse the effects of vecuronium?
questions.concept: Vecuronium is a non-depolarising neuromuscular blocker; its action is reversed by the anticholinesterase neostigmine, which raises synaptic acetylcholine (usually co-administered with atropine/glycopyrrolate to block muscarinic effects).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient came to the hospital with muscle weakness, diarrhea, and bradycardia. He was diagnosed with organophosphate poisoning for which atropine was administered. After atropine administration, which of the following changes are not seen?
questions.concept: In organophosphate poisoning atropine antagonises the MUSCARINIC effects, so bradycardia is reversed (its cardinal action is to raise the heart rate) and is no longer seen. NOTE: sweating and rhinorrhoea (also muscarinic) improve too, but nicotinic muscle weakness persists because atropine has no action at the neuromuscular junction, so bradycardia is the single best 'not seen' answer despite the question being loosely worded.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient developed Achilles tendonitis and leg swelling after taking a certain antibiotic. This adverse effect is commonly associated with fluoroquinolones. What is the most likely mechanism of action of the drug involved?
options: Inhibition of bacterial DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis at 50S subunit
Inhibition of bacterial folic acid synthesis
Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis
questions.concept: Achilles tendinopathy/rupture is a classic adverse effect of fluoroquinolones, which act by inhibiting bacterial DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) and topoisomerase IV, blocking DNA replication. 50S inhibition is macrolides, folate-synthesis inhibition is sulfonamides, and cell-wall inhibition is beta-lactams.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct triple drug regimen for the treatment of Helicobacter pylori infection?
questions.concept: A standard first-line H. pylori triple regimen combines a PPI with two antibiotics; omeprazole + clarithromycin + metronidazole is a valid clarithromycin-based triple therapy. Combinations lacking a macrolide (or built on ciprofloxacin) are not standard triple therapy.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient presents with blackish discoloration of the nasal cavity and posterior buccal mucosa. He has a history of high-dose steroid use. What is the most appropriate drug for treatment?
questions.concept: Black necrotic nasal/oral mucosa in an immunosuppressed patient (high-dose steroids) suggests mucormycosis, treated with lipid/liposomal amphotericin B plus urgent surgical debridement; azoles like fluconazole and itraconazole are ineffective against Mucorales, and griseofulvin only treats dermatophytes.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: KAT G mutation associated with:
questions.concept: The katG gene encodes catalase-peroxidase, which activates the prodrug isoniazid; a katG mutation abolishes this activation and confers isoniazid resistance. Rifampicin resistance is via rpoB, fluoroquinolone via gyrA/gyrB, and ethambutol via embB.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: What is the mechanism of action of Ethosuximide?
options: Inhibits calcium channels in thalamic neurons
questions.concept: Ethosuximide, the drug of choice for absence (petit mal) seizures, works by blocking T-type calcium channels in thalamic neurons, interrupting the thalamocortical rhythm underlying 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient is brought to the emergency department with signs suggestive of opioid poisoning. What is the antidote of choice?
questions.concept: Naloxone is the opioid-receptor antagonist of choice for opioid overdose, rapidly reversing respiratory depression and miosis; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and physostigmine treats anticholinergic toxicity.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A schizophrenia patient was started on a drug and developed tremors and dystonia. Which drug is most likely responsible?
questions.concept: Typical (first-generation) antipsychotics block D2 receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway and characteristically produce extrapyramidal side effects: acute dystonia, drug-induced parkinsonism (tremor), akathisia, and later tardive dyskinesia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 68-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department in acute distress. He is diaphoretic, tachycardic, and complains of severe chest pain. His ECG is given below. Given the patient's condition, what is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
questions.concept: A haemodynamically unstable tachyarrhythmia (here atrial flutter with saw-tooth F-waves, causing distress, diaphoresis and chest pain) needs immediate synchronized DC cardioversion; antiarrhythmic drugs and ablation are for the stable or long-term setting. The instability alone dictates cardioversion regardless of the exact rhythm.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 39-year-old male presents with stress and inability to manage work-life balance. On evaluation his blood pressure is 150/95 mmHg with elevated blood sugar. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: Advise rest only, no pharmacological treatment
questions.concept: For stage 2 hypertension with hyperglycaemia, an ARB such as telmisartan is preferred because it lowers BP, is renoprotective and metabolically neutral (may even improve insulin sensitivity), unlike thiazides which can worsen glycaemia. Glucocorticoids would raise both BP and sugar, and lifestyle change alone is inadequate for stage 2 HTN.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient having hypertension is on thiazides and is complaining of fatigue and hypokalemia. Which of the following drugs can prevent potassium loss?
questions.concept: Amiloride is a potassium-sparing diuretic (it blocks the ENaC sodium channel in the collecting duct) and, added to a thiazide, offsets thiazide-induced hypokalaemia. Furosemide, acetazolamide and indapamide all waste potassium.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A group of people are travelling to the mountains, and a girl starts complaining of mountain sickness. What is the drug of choice?
questions.concept: Acetazolamide, a carbonic-anhydrase-inhibitor diuretic, is the drug of choice for prevention and treatment of acute mountain (high-altitude) sickness; it induces a mild metabolic acidosis that stimulates ventilation and speeds acclimatisation. Promethazine and dimenhydrinate treat motion sickness, not AMS.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which antihypertensive drug is contraindicated in pregnancy?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors such as enalapril are contraindicated in pregnancy: blocking the fetal renin-angiotensin system causes renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia and growth restriction. Methyldopa, labetalol and nifedipine are the safe first-line agents.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with hypertension, tachycardia and early renal involvement is prescribed an ARB (telmisartan). What is the most likely mechanism by which the drug helps improve heart rate and blood pressure?
options: By increasing sodium excretion via loop diuretics
questions.concept: ARBs such as telmisartan lower blood pressure chiefly by blocking angiotensin II at AT1 receptors, causing vasodilation and a fall in peripheral vascular resistance; the resulting BP drop can secondarily blunt reflex tachycardia. They neither block beta-1 receptors nor act as diuretics.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: Which drug is preferred for management of diabetes in a patient with cardiac and renal failure?
questions.concept: In a diabetic with heart failure and renal impairment, SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) are preferred for their proven cardio- and reno-protection. Metformin is contraindicated in advanced renal failure (lactic acidosis), pioglitazone worsens fluid overload/HF, and sulfonylureas risk hypoglycaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with osteoarthritis has taken ibuprofen for 3 months and develops occult GI bleeding. Which statement about the cause is correct?
options: PGE-1 and prostacyclin production were reduced
Mucosal injury due to inhibition of COX-2
PGE-2 and prostacyclin production were reduced
questions.concept: Ibuprofen inhibits cyclo-oxygenase, lowering gastric-protective PGE2 and prostacyclin (which normally increase mucus, bicarbonate and mucosal blood flow); loss of these prostaglandins, chiefly via COX-1, leaves the mucosa vulnerable to acid injury and bleeding. The key protective prostaglandin is PGE2, not PGE1 (option C).

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient reports recurrent skin lesions that appear within hours each time he takes an NSAID, recurring at the same site. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.concept: Well-demarcated erythematous plaques that recur at the same site within hours of a specific drug (classically NSAIDs or sulfonamides) and heal with residual hyperpigmentation define a fixed drug eruption. Erythema multiforme shows target lesions without same-site recurrence, and drug-induced pigmentation is persistent rather than acute and recurrent.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient took a drug for migraine treatment, following which there was numbness and the hand appeared discoloured (as shown). What is the possible drug that was taken?
questions.concept: Numbness and colour change of the fingers (Raynaud-like peripheral vasoconstriction that can progress to gangrene) after a migraine drug points to an ergot alkaloid such as dihydroergotamine; sumatriptan, butorphanol and aspirin do not cause this ergotism.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis is taking indomethacin and an ACE inhibitor for hypertension. What potential side effect is likely to be seen?
questions.concept: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone (reducing potassium excretion) and NSAIDs like indomethacin reduce renal prostaglandins/perfusion; together they promote potassium retention, causing hyperkalaemia.

questions.subject: Pharmacology
questions.stem: A 75 kg person is administered a drug with a half-life of 3 hours. What is the approximate clearance of the drug?
questions.concept: Clearance = 0.693 x Vd / t-half; taking the standard Vd of about 100 mL/kg (Vd ~7000 mL) and t-half = 3 h gives roughly 1600 mL/h, i.e. about 23 mL/min, the only per-minute option. NOTE: the recalled stem omits the volume of distribution, which must be assumed (~100 mL/kg) to solve it; option B (1670) is the mL/h value mislabelled as mL/min.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which structure of the brain is responsible for coordination of voluntary movements?
questions.concept: The cerebellum coordinates the timing, smoothness and accuracy of voluntary movement and maintains balance and posture; its damage causes ataxia, dysmetria and intention tremor rather than paralysis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 45-year-old patient has an absent pupillary light reflex but a preserved near (accommodation) reflex. Where is the lesion most likely located?
questions.concept: Loss of the light reflex with a preserved near reflex (light-near dissociation) localizes to the pretectal area, where the afferent light pathway reaches the Edinger-Westphal nuclei before the near-reflex (cortical) fibres join - the basis of the Argyll Robertson pupil and Parinaud syndrome. An optic-nerve or oculomotor-nerve lesion abolishes both reflexes, as would destruction of the Edinger-Westphal nucleus itself.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: An alcoholic patient presents with palpitations, dizziness and syncopal attacks. On examination the pulse is irregularly irregular. What will be seen on the JVP?
questions.concept: An irregularly irregular pulse in a chronic alcoholic points to atrial fibrillation ('holiday heart'). Because the atria fibrillate rather than contract in a coordinated way, the atrial-systole 'a' wave of the JVP disappears. A large a wave is seen in tricuspid stenosis/pulmonary hypertension, a cannon a wave in AV dissociation (complete heart block/VT), and a steep y descent in constrictive pericarditis.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: In the jugular venous pressure (JVP) waveform, the 'a' wave corresponds to:
options: Tricuspid valve bulging into Right atria
questions.concept: The 'a' wave of the jugular venous pulse is produced by right atrial contraction (just after the P wave, before S1). The 'c' wave reflects tricuspid bulging in early ventricular systole and the 'v' wave reflects atrial filling against a closed tricuspid valve.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: A patient presents with high blood pressure accompanied by a decrease in heart rate. What is the most likely physiological mechanism responsible for this response?
questions.concept: A rise in blood pressure stretches carotid-sinus and aortic-arch baroreceptors, increasing afferent firing (via CN IX and X) to the medulla; the reflex withdraws sympathetic tone and raises vagal tone, lowering the heart rate. This baroreceptor reflex buffers acute changes in blood pressure.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: Which enzyme is responsible for conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II?
questions.concept: Angiotensin-converting enzyme, found mainly on pulmonary vascular endothelium, cleaves angiotensin I to the potent vasoconstrictor angiotensin II (and also degrades bradykinin): the step blocked by ACE inhibitors.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.topic: Cardiac cycle, ECG basis, BP regulation
questions.stem: Which phase of the cardiac cycle corresponds to the first heart sound (S1)?
questions.concept: The first heart sound (S1) is produced by closure of the mitral and tricuspid (AV) valves at the very start of ventricular systole, which marks the onset of isovolumetric contraction.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which among the following hormones, in a lactating mother, is responsible for the growth of breast tissue?
questions.concept: In a lactating mother prolactin drives lobuloalveolar growth of breast tissue and milk synthesis, while oxytocin causes milk ejection. NOTE: estrogen (ductal growth) and progesterone (alveolar growth) also enlarge the breast, but the lactation-specific answer intended here is prolactin.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which among the following hormones acts on post ovulatory endometrium?
questions.concept: After ovulation the corpus luteum secretes progesterone, which converts the oestrogen-primed proliferative endometrium into the secretory phase to support implantation.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which hormone is primarily responsible for increasing basal metabolic rate?
questions.concept: Thyroid hormone (T4/T3) is the principal determinant of basal metabolic rate, increasing mitochondrial oxidative metabolism, Na+/K+-ATPase activity and heat production across most tissues.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: A 12-year-old girl has Tanner stage II breast development and a white, odourless vaginal discharge. This discharge is most likely due to which hormone?
questions.concept: Rising oestrogen in early puberty makes the vaginal epithelium proliferate and produce glycogen, which lactobacilli convert to lactic acid, giving a normal white, odourless physiological leukorrhoea. GnRH and inhibin B act on the pituitary/gonadal axis without directly producing this discharge (and 'B-Lynch suture' is a surgical technique - an erroneous distractor).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What is the primary protein that binds to thyroxine?
questions.concept: Thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG) is the principal, highest-affinity plasma carrier of thyroid hormones and transports the majority of circulating T4/T3; transthyretin (prealbumin) and albumin carry smaller fractions.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: As a neuron's diameter increases, what effect manifests?
questions.concept: Increasing axon diameter lowers internal (axial) resistance, letting local currents spread faster along the fibre, so conduction velocity increases. Action-potential amplitude is set by ion-channel and equilibrium-potential properties, not diameter.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What is the typical Glomerular Filtration Rate (GFR) in a healthy adult?
questions.concept: Normal glomerular filtration rate in a healthy adult is about 125 mL/min (roughly 180 L/day), conventionally estimated using inulin or creatinine clearance.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: In a renal biopsy, identify the cells located in the angle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, adjacent to the macula densa.
questions.concept: Cells lying in the angle between the afferent and efferent arterioles, adjacent to the macula densa, are the extraglomerular mesangial (lacis/Goormaghtigh) cells of the juxtaglomerular apparatus, which relay signals between the macula densa and renin-secreting JG cells. Macula densa lies in the distal tubule and JG cells in the afferent arteriole wall.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: What renal function is represented by the formula UV/P?
questions.concept: Renal clearance is calculated as (U x V)/P - urine concentration times urine flow rate divided by plasma concentration - giving the volume of plasma completely cleared of a substance per unit time.

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which part of the nephron is impermeable to water?
options: Descending limb of loop of Henle
Ascending limb of loop of Henle
questions.concept: The thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle is impermeable to water but actively reabsorbs Na+/K+/2Cl-, diluting the tubular fluid and building the medullary osmotic gradient that drives water reabsorption elsewhere (the countercurrent mechanism).

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Dehydration is more severe in infants than in adults. Which of the following is a true statement about infants?
options: Extracellular fluid (ECF) is more than intracellular fluid (ICF)
Total body water in infants is more than in adults
Intracellular fluid (ICF) is more than extracellular fluid (ECF)
questions.concept: Infants have a higher total body water fraction (about 75-80% of body weight vs about 60% in adults) and a higher water turnover, which is why they dehydrate faster. (ECF exceeds ICF at birth, but ICF comes to predominate after the first year.)

questions.subject: Physiology
questions.stem: Which of the following factors causes a rightward shift in the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve?
questions.concept: A rightward shift of the oxygen-haemoglobin dissociation curve means lower O2 affinity and easier tissue unloading. It is produced by increased CO2 and H+ (low pH, the Bohr effect), increased temperature and increased 2,3-BPG.
